![](../../img/conversation_2780E3.svg){.page-art}

*An in-class activity. Nothing to turn in and no answer key -- this one needs
other people, which is why it happens in class rather than at home.*

**The idea.** The 95% in a 95% confidence interval is a property of the
*procedure*, not of the one interval in front of you. One person cannot see that;
a roomful of people running the same procedure can.

**Format.** About 15 minutes · pairs · one laptop per pair.

## 1. Commit, on your own (2 minutes)

We will each draw 100 samples of $n = 25$ from a population whose mean is *known*
to be 100 and build a 95% interval from each. Write down numbers, not ranges:

a) How many of your 100 intervals will contain 100?
b) How much will your neighbour's answer differ from yours?

## 2. Run your own (7 minutes)

Set the seed to your own number, so that no two pairs in the room get the same
result.

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)   # <- your own number here
n <- 25

sims <- tibble(rep = 1:100) |>
  mutate(
    sample = map(rep, \(i) rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 15)),
    xbar = map_dbl(sample, mean),
    se = map_dbl(sample, \(x) sd(x) / sqrt(n)),
    lower = xbar - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
    upper = xbar + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
    covers = lower <= 100 & 100 <= upper
  )

sum(sims$covers)                     # your coverage count
mean(sims$upper - sims$lower)        # your average width

ggplot(sims, aes(y = rep, x = xbar, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, color = covers)) +
  geom_pointrange(linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100)
```

Re-run with `n <- 100` and record both numbers again. Bring four numbers to the
board: coverage and width, at each sample size.

## 3. Assemble the class (6 minutes)

Every pair's four numbers go up. Then, together:

- What is the range of coverage counts in the room? Nobody's individual run tells
  you that, and it is the actual behaviour of the method.
- Which column changed when $n$ went to 100, and which did not?
- Point at the pair with the *lowest* coverage. Did they do anything wrong?
- In real research you get one interval and no vertical line. Looking at the
  board, could any single pair have known which kind they had?

*If you have more time: swap the population for `rexp(n, rate = 1/100)` at
$n = 25$ and re-pool. Coverage drops for the whole room. Which part broke?*

{{< dstart summary="If you were not in class" >}}

The room's coverage counts scatter around 95 -- typically from about 89 to 99 --
and the pair at the bottom did nothing wrong. Going to $n = 100$ leaves the
coverage column alone and halves the width column. **Coverage is what the method
promises; width is what your sample size buys.**

The board is the argument. From inside one run there is no signal at all about
whether you are one of the 95 or one of the 5, which is exactly why "there is a
95% chance the true value is in *this* interval" does not follow from the
procedure's guarantee -- and why reading it off a single plot in a textbook never
quite convinces anyone.

On the extension: nothing is wrong with the standard error or the $t$ multiplier.
What fails is the assumption that the sampling distribution of the mean is
*already* near normal at $n = 25$ when the population is badly skewed.
